text: # Finneas on Producing Billie Eilish’s Hit Album in his Bedroom Los Angeles, CA (May 23, 2019)—Much has been made of the fact that virtually everything Billie Eilish has released with her co-writer, producer and older brother Finneas O’Connell was recorded in his bedroom at the family home. That’s hardly surprising when you consider her career trajectory, going from a song posted in late 2015 to Soundcloud for a dance class that blew up almost overnight to becoming the first artist born in the 21st century to have a Number-One album on the _Billboard_ 200, in early April 2019. In the intervening three and a half years, Eilish (full name: Billie Eilish Pirate Baird O’Connell) racked up one billion on-demand streams before releasing her debut full-length, _When We All Fall Asleep, Where Do We Go?_—Nielsen Music reported that she had passed 3.79 billion streams by April 25—and has seen 12 of the 14 album tracks, plus two other songs, hit _Billboard_’s Hot 100. Not bad for a 17-year-old who, incidentally, is now the youngest female ever to have a Number-One album in the UK. “People have put a lot of emphasis on that room as part of our lineage,” says O’Connell on the phone from Australia during a tour leg on which he both opened for, as a solo artist, and performed with Eilish. “It was lovely to make an album there, but I think it’s really important to work wherever you are, or wherever you have your tools.” This is no humblebrag bedroom studio that turns out to have been professionally outfitted. It’s just a regular bedroom, with a bed against one wall, where Eilish sat to record her vocals, facing a desk and bookshelves and O’Connell’s modest production setup: Apple Logic Pro X, a Universal Audio Apollo 8 interface and a pair of Yamaha HS5 nearfields with an H8S subwoofer. O’Connell, who turns 22 in July, has since moved out, setting up a duplicate, slightly upgraded collection of gear at his new home, including a pair of Yamaha HS8 monitors and an Apollo X. ![Finneas. Photo: Teren Mabry](https://www.mixonline.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/6-P18-R-Finneas-copy.jpg) Finneas. Photo: Teren Mabry As his sole reference, O’Connell says he didn’t really think about the way the bedroom sounded until he started recording elsewhere. “The bedroom has a very specific sound, very tight and intimate and closed and quiet. I love the way it makes vocals sound.” Eilish’s next album could potentially sound a little different. “All of my solo material, I record at my new house. I’m sure Billie and I will start recording there whenever we get back into recording mode for the next record,” he says. “But even if we never record full albums there again, maybe sometimes there will be just a vocal that we feel we must record in that room just to make it sound that way.” Eilish’s hip-hop-influenced yet pan-genre songs (she calls it simply “Billie Eilish music”) sometimes feature heavily effected vocals, and harmonies that are equal in level to the lead—not to mention sound effects such as an Easy-Bake oven, dentist drill and audience reaction. “Especially in a song like ‘Bad Guy,’ the thing that’s interesting isn’t necessarily the vocal melody on the verses; it’s that there’s three-part harmony and it’s the rhythm,” says O’Connell. The secret behind some of those vocal effects is Logic Pro X’s Vocal Transformer plug-in, he reveals. “It’s really good at making a vocal sound crazy and unique. It’s not necessarily the most intuitive plug-in, but if you twiddle the knobs and change some dials, it makes things really interesting. That’s the plug-in I use on ‘Bad Guy’ for the ‘rattlesnake’ vocal.” ﻿ Other than that, he says, “I use really harsh tremolo a lot. It’s set to zero percent smooth, so it’s chopping the signal, and I’ll set it to eighth- or sixteenth-note values, then set the depth.” When initially working together, a period that included the production of songs such as “Ocean Eyes,” “Six Feet Under” and “Bellyache,” O’Connell used an Audio-Technica AT2020 cardioid condenser mic on his sister’s vocals. More recently, he has been using a Neumann TLM 103 large diaphragm mic. “I recommend the TLM 103 to anyone; it’s such a good microphone.” But when he has some free time, he says, “I’ll probably do a microphone shootout somewhere and try a bunch of different things.” In fact, he bought a pair of TLM 103s and hopes to use them to record his piano eventually, but for Eilish’s productions, he has always used virtual instruments, such as Keyscape by Spectrasonics. “It’s amazing, especially the Dark Indie upright pianos. My piano in my parents’ room is not situated well for recording. It’s more fun to write on it, then record on a MIDI keyboard, especially because I like tweaking MIDI parts, changing and perfecting them.” O’Connell hands Eilish’s songs off to mixer Rob Kinelski. “Everything that I’ve sent that he’s mixed is pre-compressed and pre-panned, and all the reverbs and all the delays are pretty much already there. I’m not looking for Rob to ‘fix’ anything; he just makes it a little more balanced, because everything comes out of my bedroom at my parents’ house with too much bass. Rob and our mastering engineer, John Greenham, make sure our stuff sounds good everywhere.” O’Connell has been using Justin Hergett, a Grammy-nominated mixer and engineer who has long worked with Tony Maserati as chief engineer of Mirrorball Entertainment’s Outfit 27 team, to mix his solo work, as well as projects with artists such as Ashe, whose four-song EP he executive produced. “Hergett is really fast,” he says. “It’s fun to go into the room with the mixer and watch what they do; he’s always been very nice about letting me do that.” While Finneas O’Connell can now afford to employ a mixer and mastering engineer on his productions, it wasn’t always that way. But lack of a budget should not be a barrier to anyone starting out in the business, he says. Take “Ocean Eyes,” for example—the song that went viral and caught the attention of the management team and record label now behind Eilish. “It was mixed and mastered by me and uploaded to Soundcloud. And that song saved our lives,” says O’Connell. ﻿ “When I was starting to make music, I thought I had to pay a bunch of people to do all my things professionally and that that would be the only way I would ever have any success. It’s really important for kids to not think that there’s something intangible and out of reach for them. The truth is that you just have to make a song that people like.” Billie Eilish • [https://site.billieeilish.com](https://site.billieeilish.com) Finneas • [www.finneasofficial.com](http://www.finneasofficial.com)

# “I’m just a puppet when it comes to comping her vocal”: FINNEAS taught Billie Eilish how to comp vocals so she could record alone in new album Hit Me Hard and Soft

“I was just like, well, let me teach you how to do this. It’s not that hard,” says the producer.

![FINNEAS and Billie Eilish](https://musictech.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/Billie-Eilish-Finneas@2000x1500.jpg)

Image: Apple Music via YouTube

In a new interview, [Billie Eilish](https://musictech.com/artists/billie-eilish/) takes us behind the scenes of the making of _Hit Me Hard and Soft_, and the evolving musical partnership she shares with her brother [FINNEAS](https://musictech.com/news/music/finneas-rick-rubin-being-master-delegator-producer/).

Diving into the album’s recording process, FINNEAS – Eilish’s longtime production partner – tells Apple Music’s Zane Lowe that he actually taught his sister how to comp her own vocals this time so she could record alone in the studio.

*   **READ MORE: [Steve Albini’s four-hour Mix with the Masters lesson is now available to watch for free](https://musictech.com/news/music/steve-albini-mix-with-the-masters-free/)**

“She has such a good ear and I’m just a puppet when it comes to comping her vocals because she’s so meticulous,” says FINNEAS. “And I can comp a vocal, no prob, I’m doing it forever. But she got better and better at knowing like, ‘I like this take and I like this word from this, taking like this word’.”

“And so I was just like, well, let me teach you how to do this. It’s not that hard. And so I taught her how to record herself and how to comp herself.”

“\[Sometimes\] I’d get a call to come downstairs, she’s like ‘something’s wrong come downstairs and fix it’,” he continues, “but one of the reasons I did it is because I’ve always recorded alone and there’s stuff that I am just not brave enough to do in front of somebody else. It’s like I know I’m her brother but…”

It’s a sentiment Eilish shares in. Highlighting a vocal moment near the end of the track _Birds Of A Feather_, the singer says that she “could never have done that” had FINNEAS been in the room.

“This is the most I’ve ever written and contributed,” says Eilish. “I did some production stuff, even. And I did all my own vocals.”

Watch the full interview below.

In other news, Billie Eilish has released an [isolated vocals version of _HIT ME HARD AND SOFT_ for producers to get creative with](https://musictech.com/news/music/billie-eilish-isolated-vocals-album-remix-bandlab-interscope/). Fans are invited to remix the album via BandLab and the winner will get to “take home an exclusive merch pack with a _HIT ME HARD AND SOFT_ vinyl autographed by Billie, and a pair of tickets to her upcoming tour.”

![Crystal Koe](https://musictech.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/cropped-Crystal-author-bio-photo-400x400.jpg)

Crystal Koe is a Singapore-based writer covering music and gear news for Guitar.com and MusicTech.com since 2021. A former choir kid with an unhealthy karaoke habit, she once ran an online store peddling earphones to strangers on the internet. Her music taste runs wide — from punk and pop-rock to cool jazz and creepy film scores — and she thinks everyone should listen to Kill The Poor by Dead Kennedys at least once before they die.

# Billie Eilish’s Brother Finneas O’Connell Reveals the Secret Sounds Mixed Into Her Songs

![Finneas, Billie Eilish](https://akns-images.eonline.com/eol_images/Entire_Site/202014/rs_1024x759-200204072511-1024x759-finneas-billie-gj-2-4-20.jpg?fit=around%7C1024:759&output-quality=90&crop=1024:759;center,top)Andrew Lipovsky/NBC, Steve Granitz/WireImage

**Finneas O'Connell** is a musical genius, _duh_.

On Monday, **Billie Eilish**'s older brother stopped by _The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon_, where the 22-year-old [Grammy-winning producer and songwriter](https://www.eonline.com/photos/30140/grammy-awards-2020-candid-moments/992450) broke down his process for host **Jimmy Fallon**, revealing that [the brother-sister duo](https://www.eonline.com/videos/302236/billie-eilish-finneas-celebrate-early-grammy-wins) loves to incorporate everyday sounds into their music.

"So, I'll walk around with—just an iPhone will work—but sometimes I'll bring, like, a little mobile recorder and I'll just, like, if hear an interesting sound, I'll just record it," he said. "And then later, I'll listen through them and I'll go like, ‘I wonder how can I use that?'"

For Finneas, the method comes from wanting his music to have an original spin. "Well, I mean, because, like, computers and everything have gotten so much cheaper and accessible," he explained. "I feel like a lot of music producers have, like, the same toolbox. And I think, like, to me, as a producer, like, I want something to set my stuff apart."

Excited to give Jimmy an example of when his recordings made their way into a song, Finneas recalled an interesting one that Billie obtained from the dentist, which they incorporated into [their song "Bury A Friend."](https://www.eonline.com/news/1032619/billie-eilish-forgot-her-lyrics-during-coachella-debut-and-the-crowd-loved-it)

"We both have, like, Invisalign, like, dental teeth straighteners and she was at the dentist and they were, like grinding down…with that, like, horrible, like—whatever ASMR is, like, it's the opposite of that. Like, the most unpleasant," he said. "And so she came home from one of those appointments and was like, ‘I recorded it!' And I was like, ‘Great!' And we put it right in ‘Bury A Friend.'"

With his laptop ready, Jimmy compared the original recording of the dental drilling tool to the song and was blown away. Looking through Finneas' sound catalog, he asked him explain some of the other recordings that found their way into the musicians' [Grammy-winning album _when we all fall asleep, where do we go?_](https://www.eonline.com/news/1116128/billie-eilish-just-made-so-much-history-at-the-2020-grammys-with-all-her-wins)

For the entry labeled "crosswalk," Finneas shared that the sound came from the noise that played while pressing a crosswalk button in Australia. "That's just, every time you cross a street in Australia, you hear that," he told Jimmy. Then, he revealed that the rhythmic sound was later used in the chorus of [their song "Bad Guy."](https://www.eonline.com/photos/29726/the-biggest-and-best-songs-of-2019/982093)

Jimmy wasn't the only person stunned by this revelation. After playing the chorus and hearing the crosswalk button sound play, the cameras caught **The Roots**' drummer **Questlove** with his jaw dropped.

Switching gears, Jimmy asked Finneas, who has written for musicians like **Selena Gomez**, **Halsey**, **Camila Cabello** and more, to explain his songwriting process and how he can tell which song should to the artists he's working with.

"Well, predominately, if I'm writing for another artist, I'm sitting there with them and we're writing it together," he said. "So, that kind of works itself out, right? ‘Cuz they're in the room and we're talking about their lives." But when it comes to Billie, he shared that he'd give any song to his little sister because of how talented she is.

"Her voice just makes any song sound better to me," he gushed. "And so, if she wants a song, I'm like, ‘Take it. It'll be better if you do it.' The only ones I really keep are ones where I'm like, ‘This is like a diary entry.' It's so personal that, like, I feel like only I can sing it—even though, like, her voice would sound better on it, but it's the story of my life."

Before concluding the interview, Finneas teased the project that he and Billie just wrapped up: The [_James Bond_ theme song for _No Time To Die_](https://www.eonline.com/news/1111580/billie-eilish-makes-history-with-james-bond-no-time-to-die-theme-song). "I'm so excited," he dished, who then realized that he couldn't reveal too much. "One of the double-O agents is in the crowd and I get a hypodermic dart in my neck if I say anything…I can tell you something. It's great."

Billie Eilish & Finneas Celebrate Early Grammy Wins

He did, however, say that fans [can expect the new track soon](https://www.eonline.com/videos/302227/billie-eilish-confirms-james-bond-theme-song-is-finished). Dying to know the vibe of the song, the late night host treated the "Break My Heart Again" singer to some renditions of his favorite Bond theme songs. Impressed by his extensive knowledge of the tunes, Finneas joked, "They're gonna release a compilation album but it's gonna be only you."

_No Time To Die_ hits theaters on April 10.

(E! and NBC are both part of the NBCUniversal family.)

For Finneas, the method comes from wanting his music to have an original spin. "Well, I mean, because, like, computers and everything have gotten so much cheaper and accessible," he explained. "I feel like a lot of music producers have, like, the same toolbox. And I think, like, to me, as a producer, like, I want something to set my stuff apart."

Excited to give Jimmy an example of when his recordings made their way into a song, Finneas recalled an interesting one that Billie obtained from the dentist, which they incorporated into [their song "Bury A Friend."](https://www.eonline.com/news/1032619/billie-eilish-forgot-her-lyrics-during-coachella-debut-and-the-crowd-loved-it)

"We both have, like, Invisalign, like, dental teeth straighteners and she was at the dentist and they were, like grinding down…with that, like, horrible, like—whatever ASMR is, like, it's the opposite of that. Like, the most unpleasant," he said. "And so she came home from one of those appointments and was like, ‘I recorded it!' And I was like, ‘Great!' And we put it right in ‘Bury A Friend.'"

With his laptop ready, Jimmy compared the original recording of the dental drilling tool to the song and was blown away. Looking through Finneas' sound catalog, he asked him explain some of the other recordings that found their way into the musicians' [Grammy-winning album _when we all fall asleep, where do we go?_](https://www.eonline.com/news/1116128/billie-eilish-just-made-so-much-history-at-the-2020-grammys-with-all-her-wins)

For the entry labeled "crosswalk," Finneas shared that the sound came from the noise that played while pressing a crosswalk button in Australia. "That's just, every time you cross a street in Australia, you hear that," he told Jimmy. Then, he revealed that the rhythmic sound was later used in the chorus of [their song "Bad Guy."](https://www.eonline.com/photos/29726/the-biggest-and-best-songs-of-2019/982093)

Jimmy wasn't the only person stunned by this revelation. After playing the chorus and hearing the crosswalk button sound play, the cameras caught **The Roots**' drummer **Questlove** with his jaw dropped.

Switching gears, Jimmy asked Finneas, who has written for musicians like **Selena Gomez**, **Halsey**, **Camila Cabello** and more, to explain his songwriting process and how he can tell which song should to the artists he's working with.

"Well, predominately, if I'm writing for another artist, I'm sitting there with them and we're writing it together," he said. "So, that kind of works itself out, right? ‘Cuz they're in the room and we're talking about their lives." But when it comes to Billie, he shared that he'd give any song to his little sister because of how talented she is.

"Her voice just makes any song sound better to me," he gushed. "And so, if she wants a song, I'm like, ‘Take it. It'll be better if you do it.' The only ones I really keep are ones where I'm like, ‘This is like a diary entry.' It's so personal that, like, I feel like only I can sing it—even though, like, her voice would sound better on it, but it's the story of my life."

Before concluding the interview, Finneas teased the project that he and Billie just wrapped up: The [_James Bond_ theme song for _No Time To Die_](https://www.eonline.com/news/1111580/billie-eilish-makes-history-with-james-bond-no-time-to-die-theme-song). "I'm so excited," he dished, who then realized that he couldn't reveal too much. "One of the double-O agents is in the crowd and I get a hypodermic dart in my neck if I say anything…I can tell you something. It's great."

Billie Eilish & Finneas Celebrate Early Grammy Wins

He did, however, say that fans [can expect the new track soon](https://www.eonline.com/videos/302227/billie-eilish-confirms-james-bond-theme-song-is-finished). Dying to know the vibe of the song, the late night host treated the "Break My Heart Again" singer to some renditions of his favorite Bond theme songs. Impressed by his extensive knowledge of the tunes, Finneas joked, "They're gonna release a compilation album but it's gonna be only you."

_No Time To Die_ hits theaters on April 10.

(E! and NBC are both part of the NBCUniversal family.)

text:
# Will Billie Eilish’s ‘Birds of a Feather’ Become Her Second Hot 100 No. 1 Hit?

In its 20th week on the [Billboard Hot 100](https://www.billboard.com/charts/hot-100), [Billie Eilish](https://www.billboard.com/artist/billie-eilish)‘s “Birds of a Feather” just continues to keep flying higher and higher. The _Hit Me Hard and Soft_ single, which initially debuted at No. 13 on the Hot 100 back in early June, has since taken over the set’s initial focus track “Lunch” as the biggest hit of this Eilish era.

### Explore

[

![](https://charts-static.billboard.com/img/2017/02/billie-eilish-go0-344x344.jpg)

](https://www.billboard.com/artist/billie-eilish/)

See latest videos, charts and news

This week, it jumps from No. 6 on the chart to a new peak of No. 2 — helped in large part by the debut of its official music video. The only song that remains in the way of the single becoming Eilish’s second No. 1 on the chart is Shaboozey’s “A Bar Song (Tipsy),” which remains at No. 1 for a 13th week this frame, while still leading “Birds” on each of [Streaming Songs](https://www.billboard.com/charts/streaming-songs/), [Digital Song Sales](https://www.billboard.com/charts/digital-song-sales/) and [Radio Songs](https://www.billboard.com/charts/radio-songs/).

How has the song remained so commercially potent 20 weeks into its lifespan? And will it be able to make that final jump to No. 1 on the Hot 100? _Billboard_ staffers answer these questions and more below.

**1\. Billie Eilish’s “Birds of a Feather” reaches a new peak of No. 2 on the Hot 100 this week, in its 20th week on the chart. Are you surprised at the legs (or wings) that the song has had as a pop hit?**

**Stephen Daw**: I’m very pleasantly surprised. When _Hit Me Hard and Soft_ came out in May, “Birds of a Feather” certainly stood out to me among the other tracks, but it didn’t strike me as the logical follow-up to a lead single like “Lunch.” It is an objectively good piece of pop music, I just did not foresee “Birds” having this kind of chart omnipresence five months later. 

**Kyle Denis**: I’m not surprised at all. Even though “Skinny” was my immediate favorite from _Hit Me Hard and Soft_, “Birds of a Feather” always struck me as a surefire hit. And Billie’s singles tend to stick around for weeks before peaking, so “Birds” taking 20 weeks to reach No. 2 isn’t all that strange.

**Lyndsey Havens**: Not totally. When the album first arrived, “Birds” was a favorite among many. And whether intentional or not, I think it was smart for team Eilish to hold off on promoting it as a single until recently. With an album like _Hit Me_, the songs so seamlessly flow into one another and as Eilish has said herself, she purposely held off on releasing any singles before its release so that the album could be consumed as a full project. And in doing so, she’s allowed her fans to tell her which songs they’re most connecting with, versus the other way around. A strategy like that takes time — and in this case, 20-ish weeks seems to be the magic number.

**Jason Lipshutz**: “Birds of a Feather” snuck up on me as a no-brainer, firing-on-all-cylinders pop smash, considering how the song features Eilish in a different vocal and structural mode than we’re used to hearing. Yet “Feather” is effervescent in sound and immediate in its appeal, with a mid-tempo approach that makes it an easy connector on streaming playlists and pop radio blocks; in this way, it reminds me of Miley Cyrus’ “Flowers,” another song that persisted for months near the top of the Hot 100 and crept towards that artist’s biggest-hit-yet status.

**Andrew Unterberger**: I am a little surprised, just because “Lunch” seemed like the big one for me off the bat — but “Birds of a Feather” is such a sweet moment and pretty song that once it founds its way to the center of the culture, it’s hardly shocking that it would nest there for a while.

**2\. Much of the reason for the song jumping from 6-2 on the listing this week is the debut of its new [official music video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V9PVRfjEBTI). Does the new visual add to your appreciation / understanding of the song, detract from it, or have no major impact for you?**

**Stephen Daw**: It certainly adds to my appreciation, though marginally. I really loved that Billie took a minimalist approach to the video while adding to the kind of off-kilter, occult vibe that defined so many of her previous visuals. The effects were amazing and I loved that she left it a little bit up to interpretation. That said, I don’t see this as the kind of music video that will move the needle for people who were on the fence about the song — if you were already into “Birds of a Feather” (or not into it, for that matter), then I doubt the video is going to change that.

**Kyle Denis**: It’s not my favorite music video from Billie, but I appreciate the decision to never actually show the person she’s “sticking together” with. Overall, the clip has no major impact on my enjoyment or understanding of the song, but it does help “Birds” retain a bit of the intimacy it sacrificed on its way to becoming a genuine hit single.

**Lyndsey Havens**: It’s been a minute since I’ve seen a music video create so much discourse — and not really in the most positive way. The reaction among many seemed to be confusion, not quite understanding the visual or expecting Eilish to go in a different, perhaps more floral-inspired, direction. Either way, the video accomplished what it likely set out to do: get people talking. And as a result, it reached new heights on the Hot 100. That’s a win any way you spin it. 

**Jason Lipshutz**: The music video adds to my appreciation, in the same way that most of Eilish’s visuals have deepened the meaning of her biggest hits. She remains one of the more visually striking pop superstars working today, an A-lister whose music videos really matter by often offering something unexpected in relation to the music. The “Feather” clip is simple enough but also breathtaking in terms of visual effects, with Eilish defying gravity in an empty room; the music video grabs your attention while also placing the emotion of the song front and center.

**Andrew Unterberger**: It adds a little. I don’t think it’s one anyone expected or even really wanted from the visual — the song seemed to call out for something more lush and sentimental — but that ability and willingness to curve expectations and follow her own muse has long been a hallmark of Eilish’s stardom and artistry, and the gravity-defying, wind-swept, still incredibly personal and striking images from this more minimal clip will I think still end up being iconic of this era.

**3\. Perhaps surprisingly for a pop star of her stature, “Birds” is only Billie’s third top two hit on the Hot 100 (after “Bad Guy” and “Therefore I Am”). Do you think it will be remembered as one of the defining songs of her career, or is it too difficult to judge the overall impact of Eilish’s songs by their chart placement?**

**Stephen Daw**: I think it’s too hard to call based solely on chart performance. Just look at her other top two hits — while “Bad Guy” is such a clear, career-defining smash for Billie, “Therefore I Am” doesn’t feel like one of the five songs I would list when asked what Billie’s most definitive tracks are. Songs like “Happier Than Ever,” “When the Party’s Over,” “Bury a Friend” or “Ocean Eyes” would take those spots up for me, and they didn’t crack the chart’s top 10. Maybe “Birds” could take on that level of prominence as her career continues, but for the moment, it feels too early to tell. 

**Kyle Denis**: “Birds” will almost certainly be remembered as one of Billie’s defining songs; it takes the somber introspection of her best tracks and transposes it through the lens of grade-A pop songwriting. It’s also an endlessly applicable love song that can work for both platonic and romantic relationships. Billie’s most impactful songs — “Lovely” (with Khalid), “When the Party’s Over,” and “Happier Than Ever,” for example – often miss the Hot 100’s top 10, but “Birds of a Feather” seems to be following in the steps of “Bad Guy” with its combination of commercial success and cultural impact. 

**Lyndsey Havens**: The thing I love about Billie is when I think of her today or how she’ll be remembered in the future, it’s often for being Billie Eilish. Not for any one album or any one song or even any one hair color (though her debut lime green look is burned into memory). I don’t know if “Birds” will become a career-defining hit — and don’t necessarily think it will — but that’s fine. I think some artists’ legacies transcend their chart histories, and I believe Eilish to be one of them. 

**Jason Lipshutz**: At this point, “Birds of a Feather” is only second to “Bad Guy” as Eilish’s defining hit, surpassing songs like “Happier Than Ever,” “Everything I Wanted” and “Therefore I Am” in terms of cultural impact and chart longevity. It’s funny to think about how “Lunch” was positioned as the focus track from _Hit Me Hard and Soft_ upon its release, and listeners simply selected “Feather” as the album’s true standout through their streaming selections. Now, I could see “Feather” as a go-to track for any casual Eilish fan — or as a set-closing moment on her future arena tours.

**Andrew Unterberger**: Certainly Eilish’s chart peaks do not always correlate to cultural relevance — despite its Hot 100 bow, I don’t know if anyone considers “Therefore I Am” one of her 20 best or most impactful songs — but it does feel like “Birds” will hold a special place in her catalog, unlikely to be supplanted or replaced. [

![](https://charts-static.billboard.com/img/2017/02/billie-eilish-go0-344x344.jpg)

](https://www.billboard.com/artist/billie-eilish/)

See latest videos, charts and news

This week, it jumps from No. 6 on the chart to a new peak of No. 2 — helped in large part by the debut of its official music video. The only song that remains in the way of the single becoming Eilish’s second No. 1 on the chart is Shaboozey’s “A Bar Song (Tipsy),” which remains at No. 1 for a 13th week this frame, while still leading “Birds” on each of [Streaming Songs](https://www.billboard.com/charts/streaming-songs/), [Digital Song Sales](https://www.billboard.com/charts/digital-song-sales/) and [Radio Songs](https://www.billboard.com/charts/radio-songs/).

**Kyle Denis**: I’m not surprised at all. Even though “Skinny” was my immediate favorite from _Hit Me Hard and Soft_, “Birds of a Feather” always struck me as a surefire hit. **Lyndsey Havens**: Not totally. When the album first arrived, “Birds” was a favorite among many. A strategy like that takes time — and in this case, 20-ish weeks seems to be the magic number.

**Jason Lipshutz**: “Birds of a Feather” snuck up on me as a no-brainer, firing-on-all-cylinders pop smash, considering how the song features Eilish in a different vocal and structural mode than we’re used to hearing. **Andrew Unterberger**: I am a little surprised, just because “Lunch” seemed like the big one for me off the bat — but “Birds of a Feather” is such a sweet moment and pretty song that once it founds its way to the center of the culture, it’s hardly shocking that it would nest there for a while.

**2\. Much of the reason for the song jumping from 6-2 on the listing this week is the debut of its new [official music video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V9PVRfjEBTI). Does the new visual add to your appreciation / understanding of the song, detract from it, or have no major impact for you?**

**Stephen Daw**: It certainly adds to my appreciation, though marginally. I really loved that Billie took a minimalist approach to the video while adding to the kind of off-kilter, occult vibe that defined so many of her previous visuals. The effects were amazing and I loved that she left it a little bit up to interpretation. That said, I don’t see this as the kind of music video that will move the needle for people who were on the fence about the song — if you were already into “Birds of a Feather” (or not into it, for that matter), then I doubt the video is going to change that.

**Kyle Denis**: It’s not my favorite music video from Billie, but I appreciate the decision to never actually show the person she’s “sticking together” with. Overall, the clip has no major impact on my enjoyment or understanding of the song, but it does help “Birds” retain a bit of the intimacy it sacrificed on its way to becoming a genuine hit single.

**Lyndsey Havens**: It’s been a minute since I’ve seen a music video create so much discourse — and not really in the most positive way. The reaction among many seemed to be confusion, not quite understanding the visual or expecting Eilish to go in a different, perhaps more floral-inspired, direction. Either way, the video accomplished what it likely set out to do: get people talking. And as a result, it reached new heights on the Hot 100. That’s a win any way you spin it. 

**Jason Lipshutz**: The music video adds to my appreciation, in the same way that most of Eilish’s visuals have deepened the meaning of her biggest hits. She remains one of the more visually striking pop superstars working today, an A-lister whose music videos really matter by often offering something unexpected in relation to the music. The “Feather” clip is simple enough but also breathtaking in terms of visual effects, with Eilish defying gravity in an empty room; the music video grabs your attention while also placing the emotion of the song front and center.

**Andrew Unterberger**: It adds a little. I don’t think it’s one anyone expected or even really wanted from the visual — the song seemed to call out for something more lush and sentimental — but that ability and willingness to curve expectations and follow her own muse has long been a hallmark of Eilish’s stardom and artistry, and the gravity-defying, wind-swept, still incredibly personal and striking images from this more minimal clip will I think still end up being iconic of this era.

**3\. Perhaps surprisingly for a pop star of her stature, “Birds” is only Billie’s third top two hit on the Hot 100 (after “Bad Guy” and “Therefore I Am”). Do you think it will be remembered as one of the defining songs of her career, or is it too difficult to judge the overall impact of Eilish’s songs by their chart placement?**

Just look at her other top two hits — while “Bad Guy” is such a clear, career-defining smash for Billie, “Therefore I Am” doesn’t feel like one of the five songs I would list when asked what Billie’s most definitive tracks are. Songs like “Happier Than Ever,” “When the Party’s Over,” “Bury a Friend” or “Ocean Eyes” would take those spots up for me, and they didn’t crack the chart’s top 10. Maybe “Birds” could take on that level of prominence as her career continues, but for the moment, it feels too early to tell. 

**Kyle Denis**: “Birds” will almost certainly be remembered as one of Billie’s defining songs; it takes the somber introspection of her best tracks and transposes it through the lens of grade-A pop songwriting. It’s also an endlessly applicable love song that can work for both platonic and romantic relationships. Billie’s most impactful songs — “Lovely” (with Khalid), “When the Party’s Over,” and “Happier Than Ever,” for example – often miss the Hot 100’s top 10, but “Birds of a Feather” seems to be following in the steps of “Bad Guy” with its combination of commercial success and cultural impact. 

**Lyndsey Havens**: The thing I love about Billie is when I think of her today or how she’ll be remembered in the future, it’s often for being Billie Eilish. Not for any one album or any one song or even any one hair color (though her debut lime green look is burned into memory). I don’t know if “Birds” will become a career-defining hit — and don’t necessarily think it will — but that’s fine. I think some artists’ legacies transcend their chart histories, and I believe Eilish to be one of them. 

**Jason Lipshutz**: At this point, “Birds of a Feather” is only second to “Bad Guy” as Eilish’s defining hit, surpassing songs like “Happier Than Ever,” “Everything I Wanted” and “Therefore I Am” in terms of cultural impact and chart longevity. It’s funny to think about how “Lunch” was positioned as the focus track from _Hit Me Hard and Soft_ upon its release, and listeners simply selected “Feather” as the album’s true standout through their streaming selections. Now, I could see “Feather” as a go-to track for any casual Eilish fan — or as a set-closing moment on her future arena tours.

**Andrew Unterberger**: Certainly Eilish’s chart peaks do not always correlate to cultural relevance — despite its Hot 100 bow, I don’t know if anyone considers “Therefore I Am” one of her 20 best or most impactful songs — but it does feel like “Birds” will hold a special place in her catalog, unlikely to be supplanted or replaced. # Research: Billie Eilish + Finneas O'Connell — the bedroom anti-formula that became the formula for intimate pop

**Lane:** Billie Eilish & FINNEAS (sister–brother writer-producer duo). Focus: lyric writing + singing/topline. Era: 2020–2025 (with 2015–2019 origin facts where needed).

## Summary

Billie Eilish and Finneas O'Connell are the highest-profile example of a **self-contained, two-person writing unit**: no co-writer committees, one room, one producer. Their repeatable method inverts the standard pop pipeline — Finneas builds a small, sonically distinctive production sketch (often from field recordings, mouth-sounds, and bass-first ideas) and Billie writes the topline fast from real feeling, sung close-mic at near-whisper, so the track sounds like a secret told in the same room. The "formula" is deliberately anti-formula: unconventional structures (fake-out two-part songs like "Happier Than Ever"), no reverb on the lead vocal, and hooks that arrive as rhythm/bass/timbre rather than big belted melodies. On streaming, that quiet intimacy is the loudest thing in the feed: "BIRDS OF A FEATHER" was not even the label's chosen single, yet fans streamed it to a Hot 100 No. 2 peak, 52+ weeks on the chart, the most-streamed song of 2024 on Spotify globally, and the 2025 Grammy for Song of the Year. The duo themselves say the lesson is repeatable and emotional, not structural: write the song before the production, keep pace with the singer, carve out space so the voice can live, and don't chase what a "hit" is supposed to sound like.

---

## 1) Verified credentials & 2020–2025 relevance (skeptic-checked Hot 100 facts)

**Core duo facts (verified):**
- Nearly every Billie Eilish song is co-written with and produced by Finneas alone; 75–80% are written together in person at piano/guitar (Finneas, Variety 2019). [https://variety.com/2019/music/news/billie-eilish-finneas-oconnell-songwriting-1203421768/](https://variety.com/2019/music/news/billie-eilish-finneas-oconnell-songwriting-1203421768/)
- "Ocean Eyes" (2015): written by Finneas for his own band The Slightlys; he says it failed with his band "because my band sucked"; Billie sang it, they recorded it in his bedroom, uploaded to SoundCloud, and it launched the career. Mixed and mastered by Finneas alone. [https://americansongwriter.com/billie-eillish-interview/](https://americansongwriter.com/billie-eillish-interview/) and [https://www.mixonline.com/recording/finneas-on-producing-billie-eilishs-number-one-album-in-his-bedroom](https://www.mixonline.com/recording/finneas-on-producing-billie-eilishs-number-one-album-in-his-bedroom)
- 2019 debut *When We All Fall Asleep, Where Do We Go?* — recorded in Finneas's bedroom at their parents' house in Highland Park, LA (Logic Pro X, UA Apollo 8, Yamaha HS5s; vocals on an AT2020 then a Neumann TLM 103). [https://www.mixonline.com/recording/finneas-on-producing-billie-eilishs-number-one-album-in-his-bedroom](https://www.mixonline.com/recording/finneas-on-producing-billie-eilishs-number-one-album-in-his-bedroom)

**Billboard Hot 100 facts, 2020–2025 (each verified):**
1. **"bad guy"** (2019) — her only Hot 100 **No. 1** to date; it dethroned Lil Nas X's "Old Town Road" after its record 19-week run at No. 1, and had itself spent nine weeks at No. 2 before peaking (Billboard Chart Beat Podcast with Finneas). [https://www.billboard.com/pro/finneas-interview-billie-eilish-bad-guy-hit-songs-deconstructed-chart-beat-podcast/](https://www.billboard.com/pro/finneas-interview-billie-eilish-bad-guy-hit-songs-deconstructed-chart-beat-podcast/)
2. **"Therefore I Am"** (2020) — peaked **No. 2** on the Hot 100 (Billboard, via BOAF chart-beat piece: "only Billie's third top two hit… after 'Bad Guy' and 'Therefore I Am'"). [https://www.billboard.com/music/chart-beat/billie-eilish-birds-of-a-feather-become-her-second-hot-100-number-one-hit-1235795943/](https://www.billboard.com/music/chart-beat/billie-eilish-birds-of-a-feather-become-her-second-hot-100-number-one-hit-1235795943/)
3. **"Happier Than Ever"** (song, 2021) — debuted and peaked at **No. 11** (week of Aug 14, 2021), 26-week run; Billboard confirms the debut ("after debuting at No. 11 in August" it was still at No. 43 in its 20th week). [https://www.billboard.com/music/pop/finneas-happier-than-ever-grammys-2022-interview-1235012092/](https://www.billboard.com/music/pop/finneas-happier-than-ever-grammys-2022-interview-1235012092/) Note: the *album* *Happier Than Ever* debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200.
4. **"LUNCH"** (2024) — debuted at **No. 5** on the Hot 100, **her highest-ever debut** (and her highest chart placement since "Therefore I Am"); the album *HIT ME HARD AND SOFT* opened at **No. 2** on the Billboard 200 with **339,000 units — her biggest career week** — and **all 10 album tracks debuted in the Hot 100 top 40**. [https://www.billboard.com/lists/post-malone-morgan-wallen-billie-eilish-billboard-hot-100/](https://www.billboard.com/lists/post-malone-morgan-wallen-billie-eilish-billboard-hot-100/) and [https://www.billboard.com/music/chart-beat/billie-eilish-hit-me-hard-and-soft-all-songs-hot-100-top-40-1235694294/](https://www.billboard.com/music/chart-beat/billie-eilish-hit-me-hard-and-soft-all-songs-hot-100-top-40-1235694294/)
5. **"BIRDS OF A FEATHER"** (2024) — **peak No. 2 on the Hot 100** (in its 20th week, behind Shaboozey's "A Bar Song (Tipsy)" — Billboard staffers debated whether it would ever reach No. 1). **Correction for this project: it is NOT a Hot 100 No. 1.** Its No. 1s were: Billboard **Global 200** (2 weeks, her first), **Pop Airplay** (8 weeks; 50-week chart run, a record for a solo female), and Hot Rock & Alternative Songs (30+ weeks, first female-led song to do so). Other verified records: first Eilish song to spend **52+ weeks on the Hot 100** (surpassing "bad guy"'s 49); **5× Platinum** (RIAA, March 2025); **most-streamed song of 2024 on Spotify globally** (fastest to 2B and 3B streams at the time); 4th best-selling song of 2024 worldwide (IFPI). [https://www.billboard.com/music/chart-beat/billie-eilish-birds-of-a-feather-become-her-second-hot-100-number-one-hit-1235795943/](https://www.billboard.com/music/chart-beat/billie-eilish-birds-of-a-feather-become-her-second-hot-100-number-one-hit-1235795943/), [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birds_of_a_Feather_(Billie_Eilish_song)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birds_of_a_Feather_(Billie_Eilish_song)), [https://www.billboard.com/music/chart-beat/billie-eilish-birds-of-a-feather-global-charts-number-one-1235751280/](https://www.billboard.com/music/chart-beat/billie-eilish-birds-of-a-feather-global-charts-number-one-1235751280/), [https://variety.com/2025/music/news/billie-eilish-birds-of-a-feather-spotify-most-streamed-song-2024-1236263521/](https://variety.com/2025/music/news/billie-eilish-birds-of-a-feather-spotify-most-streamed-song-2024-1236263521/)
6. **"WILDFLOWER"** (2024) — debuted No. 17; still climbing in week 20 (No. 35) as a non-single ballad, "proof of a general hunger for Eilish's new music" (Billboard). [https://www.billboard.com/music/chart-beat/billie-eilish-birds-of-a-feather-become-her-second-hot-100-number-one-hit-1235795943/](https://www.billboard.com/music/chart-beat/billie-eilish-birds-of-a-feather-become-her-second-hot-100-number-one-hit-1235795943/)

**2025 accolades/performances (verified):**
- 67th Grammys (Feb 2, 2025): **Song of the Year — "BIRDS OF A FEATHER"** (Billie Eilish & Finneas O'Connell, songwriters), plus Best Pop Vocal Album for *HIT ME HARD AND SOFT* (both per Grammy.com's official winners list); performed the song live with Finneas against an Eaton Canyon backdrop. [https://www.grammy.com/awards/categories/song-of-the-year/2025/](https://www.grammy.com/awards/categories/song-of-the-year/2025/), [https://www.grammy.com/news/2025-grammys-nominations-full-winners-nominees-list/](https://www.grammy.com/news/2025-grammys-nominations-full-winners-nominees-list/), [https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/billie-eilish-finneas-2025-grammys-performance-1235249395/](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/billie-eilish-finneas-2025-grammys-performance-1235249395/)
- FireAid benefit (Jan 30, 2025) — "BIRDS OF A FEATHER" closer; 2024 Olympics Closing Ceremony performance (Aug 11, 2024) spiked the song to No. 5; SNL double performance of "BIRDS OF A FEATHER"/"WILDFLOWER" (Oct 19, 2024). [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birds_of_a_Feather_(Billie_Eilish_song)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birds_of_a_Feather_(Billie_Eilish_song))
- Prior run: "What Was I Made For?" (Barbie, 2023) won Song of the Year at the 66th Grammys and Best Original Song at the 2025 Oscars, making Eilish the youngest double-Oscar winner (Rolling Stone cover story). [https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/billie-eilish-hit-me-hard-and-soft-mental-health-fame-1235003585/](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/billie-eilish-hit-me-hard-and-soft-mental-health-fame-1235003585/)

**Guitar Songs era (2022):** surprise 2-track EP "TV" / "The 30th" (July 21, 2022). "TV" debuted live in Manchester (June 2022) and references Roe v. Wade; the line was written weeks before the ruling as "a placeholder of doom." [https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/billie-eilish-guitar-songs-ep-1386276/](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/billie-eilish-guitar-songs-ep-1386276/), [https://www.nme.com/news/music/billie-eilish-drops-guitar-songs-with-two-surprise-tracks-tv-and-the-30th-3274202](https://www.nme.com/news/music/billie-eilish-drops-guitar-songs-with-two-surprise-tracks-tv-and-the-30th-3274202)

---

## 2) The core repeatable workflow/formula — as they actually do it

**Setup: one room, two people, no committee.** Finneas: "probably 75-80% of the songs are written with us sitting next to each other at a piano or with a guitar, singing a melody together… It's like a relay race — we really feel like we both have to kill our portion of it to get to the finish line." (Variety, 2019). [https://variety.com/2019/music/news/billie-eilish-finneas-oconnell-songwriting-1203421768/](https://variety.com/2019/music/news/billie-eilish-finneas-oconnell-songwriting-1203421768/) The trust is sibling-trust: they grew up together, Finneas knows "the tapestry of each other's lives," so he can ask the right question even when she won't say much (TapeOp, 2024). [https://tapeop.com/interviews/165/finneas-oconnell](https://tapeop.com/interviews/165/finneas-oconnell) They tried outside co-writers as teenagers and rejected it: "all the songs we wrote with [others] were not as good as the songs me and Finneas wrote alone" (Billie, Variety). [https://variety.com/2019/music/news/billie-eilish-finneas-oconnell-songwriting-1203421768/](https://variety.com/2019/music/news/billie-eilish-finneas-oconnell-songwriting-1203421768/)

**Step-by-step (as documented across TapeOp, Billboard, Mix, Apple Music, Rolling Stone):**

1. **Song first, production second (in the room, in real time).** Finneas: "the song comes first… if I can write a bad song *before* devoting hours of production time into my bad idea, that is smarter." Songwriting happens live at piano/guitar — he reacts in real time ("If Billie starts to slow down, I slow down right with her. If she wants to change keys, I modulate with her") (TapeOp, 2024). [https://tapeop.com/interviews/165/finneas-oconnell](https://tapeop.com/interviews/165/finneas-oconnell)
2. **Vamp and improvise nonsense until a topline appears.** The process looks like "playing random sh–, singing in tandem, making up words and singing words that aren't even real words" (Billie, Variety 2019, describing their Stern interview demo and their normal practice). [https://variety.com/2019/music/news/billie-eilish-finneas-oconnell-songwriting-1203421768/](https://variety.com/2019/music/news/billie-eilish-finneas-oconnell-songwriting-1203421768/)
3. **Capture everything.** Original voice memos of Billie and Finneas writing "Everything I Wanted" were aired on Song Exploder (Episode 197) — the duo's voice-memo habit is part of the workflow. [https://songexploder.net/billie-eilish](https://songexploder.net/billie-eilish)
4. **Finneas scaffolds the track with distinctive sound sources first** (field recordings, everyday foley, bass/rhythm ideas), then **Billie writes the topline to the production** in many cases. Documented examples: "bad guy" began when *Billie* composed the distorted outro bassline, and the song was built around bass + kick with Billie writing lyrics over it (Rolling Stone breakdown video; FADER). [https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/billie-eilish-bad-guy-finneas-song-breakdown-video-882603/](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/billie-eilish-bad-guy-finneas-song-breakdown-video-882603/), [https://www.thefader.com/2019/12/16/watch-billie-eilish-deconstruct-the-production-of-bad-guy](https://www.thefader.com/2019/12/16/watch-billie-eilish-deconstruct-the-production-of-bad-guy) For "Therefore I Am," Finneas wrote and recorded the chorus hook in his own lower voice as a placeholder and they kept the concept: "I wrote and recorded the chorus in my own voice… and just had it as this hook. I had no idea what to do with it" (Finneas, walkthrough video, via Mixing A Band). [https://mixingaband.com/vocal-production-for-billie-eilish-by-finneas/](https://mixingaband.com/vocal-production-for-billie-eilish-by-finneas/)
5. **No reverb on the lead vocal; carve out space.** "I wanted Billie's voice to have this three-dimensionality in a song – something you could see if you closed your eyes. The only way I could do that was to carve all of this space out" (TapeOp). [https://tapeop.com/interviews/165/finneas-oconnell](https://tapeop.com/interviews/165/finneas-oconnell)
6. **Record many takes; comp manually; keep imperfection.** Billie records dozens of takes and comps them herself since 2021 ("she would make the choices, like 'This is the take, I like this take the best'" — Finneas). No Auto-Tune for pitch correction on Billie ("If there are moments where it's not exactly on the cent, that's probably great" — TapeOp). [https://www.billboard.com/music/pop/finneas-happier-than-ever-grammys-2022-interview-1235012092/](https://www.billboard.com/music/pop/finneas-happier-than-ever-grammys-2022-interview-1235012092/), [https://tapeop.com/interviews/165/finneas-oconnell](https://tapeop.com/interviews/165/finneas-oconnell)
7. **Pre-mix and hand off.** Finneas delivers pre-compressed, pre-panned stems with reverbs/delays printed; Rob Kinelski (through 2023) and Jon Castelli (HMHAS) balance it. [https://www.mixonline.com/recording/finneas-on-producing-billie-eilishs-number-one-album-in-his-bedroom](https://www.mixonline.com/recording/finneas-on-producing-billie-eilishs-number-one-album-in-his-bedroom), [https://tapeop.com/interviews/165/finneas-oconnell](https://tapeop.com/interviews/165/finneas-oconnell)

**Sibling-trust factor:** For *HIT ME HARD AND SOFT* the workflow decentralized — Finneas taught Billie to record and comp herself so she could work alone at her own home studio, with him "just a puppet when it comes to comping her vocals." Billie: "This is the most I've ever written and contributed. I did some production stuff, even. And I did all my own vocals." She recorded a vulnerable near-whispered moment in "BIRDS OF A FEATHER" that she "could never have done" with him in the room (Apple Music / Zane Lowe, via MusicTech). [https://musictech.com/news/music/finneas-billie-eilish-comping-vocals/](https://musictech.com/news/music/finneas-billie-eilish-comping-vocals/) Yet the *writing* stays two-in-a-room: the pair wrote "Happier Than Ever" sitting together on an $80 kids' toy guitar while jet-lagged in Denmark, then finished it in lockdown months later (Finneas, Billboard 2021). [https://www.billboard.com/music/pop/finneas-happier-than-ever-grammys-2022-interview-1235012092/](https://www.billboard.com/music/pop/finneas-happier-than-ever-grammys-2022-interview-1235012092/)

## 3) Lyric method — fast from feeling, diary-confession

- **Write from the real feeling of that exact moment.** "Happier Than Ever" was "correlated to what she was going through in her life at that exact moment" (Finneas). [https://www.billboard.com/music/pop/finneas-happier-than-ever-grammys-2022-interview-1235012092/](https://www.billboard.com/music/pop/finneas-happier-than-ever-grammys-2022-interview-1235012092/) The HMHAS session that produced the album's most honest writing started from a fight in which Billie told Finneas: "Just say how you feel and let's write a song about whatever you're scared about" — she called it "the first day really that I was able to be honest" (Apple Music/Zane Lowe interview). [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R-ZIRAmO60c](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R-ZIRAmO60c)
- **Songs "write themselves" when feelings surface.** "Male Fantasy" (HTE): "Afterwards, I'd listen and I'd be like, 'Oh my God, wow… Things, feelings, emotions. You don't even realize they're there until you do. It's a crazy process, this album." (Billie, Zane Lowe, 2021). [https://www.billboard.com/music/pop/billie-eilish-talks-recording-happier-than-ever-album-9598782/](https://www.billboard.com/music/pop/billie-eilish-talks-recording-happier-than-ever-album-9598782/)
- **Diary-confession as identity.** Billie: "I have overshared my whole life. It's compulsive, like I need to tell you every single detail about something." (Rolling Stone cover, 2024). [https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/billie-eilish-hit-me-hard-and-soft-mental-health-fame-1235003585/](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/billie-eilish-hit-me-hard-and-soft-mental-health-fame-1235003585/) Finneas keeps songs for himself only when "this is like a diary entry… it's the story of my life" (Tonight Show, via E!). [https://www.eonline.com/news/1119212/billie-eilish-s-brother-finneas-o-connell-reveals-the-secret-sounds-mixed-into-her-songs](https://www.eonline.com/news/1119212/billie-eilish-s-brother-finneas-o-connell-reveals-the-secret-sounds-mixed-into-her-songs)
- **Speed is real, but revision is ruthless.** Billie wrote the entire Jessie Reyez session song "in a flash" — "I just came up with this melody and all these lyrics, and then I wrote this whole song and we recorded it — it had never happened that fast for me" (Variety). [https://variety.com/2019/music/news/billie-eilish-finneas-oconnell-songwriting-1203421768/](https://variety.com/2019/music/news/billie-eilish-finneas-oconnell-songwriting-1203421768/) And yet "BIRDS OF A FEATHER" was labored over for ~7 months: "I don't think we've ever overthought a song more" (Billie); they kept a journal of rejected rhymes ("dismay," "convey," "bouquet") and rewrote the *entire chorus* at the end, landing on "And I don't know what I'm crying for / I don't think I could love you more." Finneas: "we overthought this sort of simple song so hard… we kept getting lost in the maze." (Apple Music *Story of My Song* breakdown, via Audacy). [https://www.audacy.com/new965philly/news/billie-eilish-and-finneas-share-story-of-birds-of-a-feather](https://www.audacy.com/new965philly/news/billie-eilish-and-finneas-share-story-of-birds-of-a-feather)
- **Learned structure, then deliberately broke it.** Their mother's songwriting class taught the Beatles-simple section names; "the main idea was that once you know the basics, then you can change them" (Billie). Billie can't even outline "Bury a Friend"'s structure: "Chorus, verse, prechorus, hook verse, bridge, verse, chorus — no, other bridge, then hook… I don't know… It took us months to figure out what was going on there, but it works — like, it doesn't, but it does." [https://variety.com/2019/music/news/billie-eilish-finneas-oconnell-songwriting-1203421768/](https://variety.com/2019/music/news/billie-eilish-finneas-oconnell-songwriting-1203421768/)
- **Real-life trigger → immediate song.** "Everything I Wanted" was written after Billie dreamed she killed herself: "I was in a really bad place mentally" (NYT Magazine). Finneas initially refused to write it: "I felt like an enabler in helping her write a song as bleak as that song was… the musical equivalent of giving an alcoholic another beer: 'I'm not going to support this.'" (NYT Magazine, via Business Insider). [https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2020/03/11/magazine/billie-eilish-profile.html](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2020/03/11/magazine/billie-eilish-profile.html), [https://www.businessinsider.com/billie-eilish-finneas-oconnell-everything-i-wanted-suicidal-thoughts-2020-3](https://www.businessinsider.com/billie-eilish-finneas-oconnell-everything-i-wanted-suicidal-thoughts-2020-3)
- **"TV" (2022):** first verse and chorus written months earlier on tour; the Roe v. Wade line was written weeks before the ruling as "a placeholder of doom" that became reality — a literal example of writing fast from current feeling (Zane Lowe, via NME). [https://www.nme.com/news/music/billie-eilish-drops-guitar-songs-with-two-surprise-tracks-tv-and-the-30th-3274202](https://www.nme.com/news/music/billie-eilish-drops-guitar-songs-with-two-surprise-tracks-tv-and-the-30th-3274202)
- **Co-writing with each other = one writes the scaffold, the other finishes it.** For "Everything I Wanted," Billie brought the dream; Finneas the chord world; both sing melodies back and forth ("singing a melody together"). For HMHAS, Billie "wrote and contributed" more than ever, including production, while Finneas stayed the engineer of her voice. [https://musictech.com/news/music/finneas-billie-eilish-comping-vocals/](https://musictech.com/news/music/finneas-billie-eilish-comping-vocals/)
- **Meaning belongs to the listener.** "With music, my whole thing is that it's for the listener to decide what it means. It doesn't matter what I wrote it about… as long as you interpret it the way you need to." (Billie, Apple Music breakdown). [https://www.audacy.com/new965philly/news/billie-eilish-and-finneas-share-story-of-birds-of-a-feather](https://www.audacy.com/new965philly/news/billie-eilish-and-finneas-share-story-of-birds-of-a-feather)

## 4) Topline/singing method — whisper-to-belt, close-mic, the "quiet hook"

- **The whisper is the instrument.** Her voice was "very soft" at the start; the AT2020 was too hissy for it, so Finneas upgraded to a TLM 103 and later a Telefunken ELA M 251 (chosen by Billie in a blind mic test). The soft voice dictated the gear. [https://tapeop.com/interviews/165/finneas-oconnell](https://tapeop.com/interviews/165/finneas-oconnell)
- **Close-mic, dry, no reverb = "sitting right next to Billie."** Finneas, on "bad guy": "A lot of the time, in pop music especially, there's reverb… But one of our purposes was to make it feel like you were sitting right next to Billie. You know, we made this whole album in a bedroom… my little bedroom at my parents' house had no reverb. So, we liked how the vocals felt, and we just started to embrace it." (Billboard Chart Beat Podcast). [https://www.billboard.com/pro/finneas-interview-billie-eilish-bad-guy-hit-songs-deconstructed-chart-beat-podcast/](https://www.billboard.com/pro/finneas-interview-billie-eilish-bad-guy-hit-songs-deconstructed-chart-beat-podcast/)
- **The room is a vocal effect.** "The bedroom has a very specific sound, very tight and intimate and closed and quiet. I love the way it makes vocals sound." (Finneas, Mix, 2019). [https://www.mixonline.com/recording/finneas-on-producing-billie-eilishs-number-one-album-in-his-bedroom](https://www.mixonline.com/recording/finneas-on-producing-billie-eilishs-number-one-album-in-his-bedroom)
- **Whisper-to-belt dynamics as arrangement.** "Happier Than Ever" is the canonical example: verse/chorus in a near-whisper over fingerpicked guitar, then a full-band rock second half where she screams ("the screaming she does in the ending of the song where she's literally yelling and screaming curse words" — Finneas's favorite moment of the recording). [https://www.billboard.com/music/pop/finneas-happier-than-ever-grammys-2022-interview-1235012092/](https://www.billboard.com/music/pop/finneas-happier-than-ever-grammys-2022-interview-1235012092/)
- **"BIRDS OF A FEATHER" contains the highest belt of her career** (Billie, Apple Music interview, per Capital). The first verse was "the most challenging… to sing" on the whole album — she auditioned multiple note choices per lyric (Apple Music breakdown via Audacy). [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birds_of_a_Feather_(Billie_Eilish_song)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birds_of_a_Feather_(Billie_Eilish_song)), [https://www.audacy.com/new965philly/news/billie-eilish-and-finneas-share-story-of-birds-of-a-feather](https://www.audacy.com/new965philly/news/billie-eilish-and-finneas-share-story-of-birds-of-a-feather)
- **The "quiet hook": hook = rhythm + timbre + spoken-word, not belt.** "bad guy" is built on a bassline the crowd sings like "a soccer chant"; the chorus deliberately "has no hook" in the traditional sense — "The thing we were most worried about was the chorus, and having it have no hook" (Billie). The "duh" ad-lib took an "incredibly high number of takes" (34, per Rolling Stone's breakdown coverage) and was left slightly imperfect for character. [https://www.billboard.com/pro/finneas-interview-billie-eilish-bad-guy-hit-songs-deconstructed-chart-beat-podcast/](https://www.billboard.com/pro/finneas-interview-billie-eilish-bad-guy-hit-songs-deconstructed-chart-beat-podcast/), [https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/billie-eilish-bad-guy-finneas-song-breakdown-video-882603/](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/billie-eilish-bad-guy-finneas-song-breakdown-video-882603/)
- **Melody as speech rhythm.** Finneas on "bad guy" verses: "the thing that's interesting isn't necessarily the vocal melody on the verses; it's that there's three-part harmony and it's the rhythm." [https://www.mixonline.com/recording/finneas-on-producing-billie-eilishs-number-one-album-in-his-bedroom](https://www.mixonline.com/recording/finneas-on-producing-billie-eilishs-number-one-album-in-his-bedroom)
- **Comping as a vocal-writing tool.** Billie comps takes line-by-line from memory of which take had the best word: "I like this take and I like this word from this, taking like this word" (Finneas describing her process). [https://musictech.com/news/music/finneas-billie-eilish-comping-vocals/](https://musictech.com/news/music/finneas-billie-eilish-comping-vocals/)
- **Trained dynamics (2024+).** Eilish believed she'd "always have a soft voice" until singing lessons expanded her range — "the truth is that literally the love of my life is singing. And I didn't realize that you can train that instrument" (Vogue cover, Nov 2024; NPR Fresh Air, Dec 2024). [https://freshairarchive.org/segments/billie-eilish-thought-shed-always-have-soft-voice-singing-lessons-changed](https://freshairarchive.org/segments/billie-eilish-thought-shed-always-have-soft-voice-singing-lessons-changed), [https://web.archive.org/web/20241009003956/https:/www.vogue.com/article/billie-eilish-november-2024-cover-interview](https://web.archive.org/web/20241009003956/https:/www.vogue.com/article/billie-eilish-november-2024-cover-interview)

## 5) Vocal-anchoring production — the scaffolding under the whisper

- **Field recordings as percussion/timbre (the "mouth-sounds" signature).** Finneas records sounds constantly on his iPhone: "I'll walk around with — just an iPhone will work… if I hear an interesting sound, I'll just record it. And then later, I'll listen through them and I'll go like, 'I wonder how can I use that?'" — because "a lot of music producers have… the same toolbox… I want something to set my stuff apart." (Tonight Show, via E!). Examples: the Australian crosswalk-button beep became the rhythmic pulse of "bad guy"'s chorus; the dentist drill (recorded by Billie at her own appointment) became the grating texture of "bury a friend." [https://www.eonline.com/news/1119212/billie-eilish-s-brother-finneas-o-connell-reveals-the-secret-sounds-mixed-into-her-songs](https://www.eonline.com/news/1119212/billie-eilish-s-brother-finneas-o-connell-reveals-the-secret-sounds-mixed-into-her-songs)
- **Foley discipline:** iPhone stereo hack (record video, strip audio) for location sounds; "oftentimes, I'm just looking for something textural – something that is interplaying with five other elements" (TapeOp). [https://tapeop.com/interviews/165/finneas-oconnell](https://tapeop.com/interviews/165/finneas-oconnell)
- **"Less but chosen" production:** he now uses fewer, more intentional elements ("I know what thing is going to go the extra mile"), blending soft layers that leave "oxygen" around the voice. [https://tapeop.com/interviews/165/finneas-oconnell](https://tapeop.com/interviews/165/finneas-oconnell)
- **Signature plug-ins:** Logic's Vocal Transformer for the "rattlesnake" vocal on "bad guy"; harsh zero-percent-smooth tremolo chopped to 8th/16th notes; Valhalla Room/VintageVerb and EchoBoy for the rare reverb/delay. [https://www.mixonline.com/recording/finneas-on-producing-billie-eilishs-number-one-album-in-his-bedroom](https://www.mixonline.com/recording/finneas-on-producing-billie-eilishs-number-one-album-in-his-bedroom), [https://tapeop.com/interviews/165/finneas-oconnell](https://tapeop.com/interviews/165/finneas-oconnell)
- **Keep the mistakes that give life:** the humming at the top of "bad guy" was kept against Finneas's instinct because it makes the bass seem in a different key — "No, no, no" (Billie); breaths had to be "exactly the same." [https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/billie-eilish-bad-guy-finneas-song-breakdown-video-882603/](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/billie-eilish-bad-guy-finneas-song-breakdown-video-882603/)
- **Easter-egg sourcing:** on "BIRDS OF A FEATHER," a heavily edited snippet of Billie's own "Getting Older" vocal was chopped into the production — the duo discovered it mid-breakdown (Apple Music *Story of My Song*). [https://www.audacy.com/new965philly/news/billie-eilish-and-finneas-share-story-of-birds-of-a-feather](https://www.audacy.com/new965philly/news/billie-eilish-and-finneas-share-story-of-birds-of-a-feather)
- **Live quietness reinforces the studio sound:** no monitor wedges on stage because Billie sings quietly; amps backstage, drummer behind plexiglass — the live show preserves the whisper aesthetic (TapeOp). [https://tapeop.com/interviews/165/finneas-oconnell](https://tapeop.com/interviews/165/finneas-oconnell)

## 6) Proof songs (2020–2025 focus)

**"Happier Than Ever" (2021)** — the fake-out structure, documented. Started in 2019 on an $80 toy guitar in Middelfart, Denmark ("I had this little toy guitar… It just sounded really cute"); the "When I'm away from you, I'm happier than ever" chorus melody came first, tied to what Billie was going through "at that exact moment"; finished in lockdown 2020 (8 months later they "wrote what became part two" — acoustically); recording completed summer 2020. The song is a whisper-to-scream two-part structure: fingerpicked guitar + intimate verse, then a full-band rock outro with screamed curse words — Finneas: "We found it cathartic. We were like, 'Oh, this is definitely the title track.'" Chart: Hot 100 debut/peak #11 (Aug 2021), 26 weeks. (Billboard Finneas interview; elpee.jp chart archive). [https://www.billboard.com/music/pop/finneas-happier-than-ever-grammys-2022-interview-1235012092/](https://www.billboard.com/music/pop/finneas-happier-than-ever-grammys-2022-interview-1235012092/), [https://billboard.elpee.jp/single/Happier%20Than%20Ever/Billie%20Eilish](https://billboard.elpee.jp/single/Happier%20Than%20Ever/Billie%20Eilish)

**"BIRDS OF A FEATHER" (2024)** — the over-thought "simple" song; proof that a soft mid-tempo love song can be the biggest song of the year. D major, 105 BPM; title reverses the cliché (everyone sings about dying for love; "I want you to stay / Till I'm in the grave / Till I rot away, dead and buried" flips it to *wanting to die after* the loved one — Finneas: "There's a lot of songs about dying for somebody and loving them till they die, and I thought it was really fun to reverse it"). Written Feb 2023–Jan 2024; ~7 months of deliberation; chorus rewritten at the end; contains her highest belt to date; features a Finneas-sung or heavily-produced vocal stack and a chopped "Getting Older" sample. Result: fan-chosen hit — peaked #2 Hot 100, #1 Global 200 (2 wks), 52+ weeks Hot 100, Spotify's most-streamed song of 2024, 2025 Grammy Song of the Year. [https://www.audacy.com/new965philly/news/billie-eilish-and-finneas-share-story-of-birds-of-a-feather](https://www.audacy.com/new965philly/news/billie-eilish-and-finneas-share-story-of-birds-of-a-feather), [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birds_of_a_Feather_(Billie_Eilish_song)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birds_of_a_Feather_(Billie_Eilish_song)), [https://www.vulture.com/article/billie-eilish-birds-of-a-feather-hot-100.html](https://www.vulture.com/article/billie-eilish-birds-of-a-feather-hot-100.html)

**"LUNCH" (2024)** — the "bad guy"-descendant bass banger; proof the duo can still do thumping hooks. Lo-fi bass-heavy beat; written across her real-life experience — "I wrote some of it before even doing anything with a girl, and then wrote the rest after" (Rolling Stone). Released as the post-album single 12 hours after the album dropped; debuted #5 (highest debut of her career). [https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/billie-eilish-hit-me-hard-and-soft-mental-health-fame-1235003585/](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/billie-eilish-hit-me-hard-and-soft-mental-health-fame-1235003585/), [https://www.vulture.com/article/billie-eilish-birds-of-a-feather-hot-100.html](https://www.vulture.com/article/billie-eilish-birds-of-a-feather-hot-100.html)

**Supporting proof:** "bad guy" (2019; bass-first construction, 34-take "duh," no-hook chorus, #1 Hot 100); "Everything I Wanted" (2019/20; dream-to-song in one day; Song Exploder Ep. 197; Record of the Year Grammy 2021); "TV"/"The 30th" (2022; Guitar Songs era, lyrics from current feeling, placeholders becoming real); "Therefore I Am" (2020; Finneas wrote the chorus hook in his own voice first, #2 Hot 100).
